before: A linear gradient is a generated CSS image with colors arranged along a direction.

The HTML supplies the elements; CSS supplies their presentation. This small fixture uses horizontal writing and left-to-right direction. ```html
Trail log
``` ```css .demo { writing-mode: horizontal-tb; direction: ltr; } .banner { width: 240px; height: 80px; background-image: linear-gradient(to right, navy 0%, teal 100%); } .banner span { color: white; background: black; } ```

background-image: linear-gradient(to right, navy 0%, teal 100%); is a declaration. linear-gradient is a CSS image function; parentheses hold comma-separated arguments: direction, first color stop, last color stop. to right points toward the physical right; 0% and 100% are positions along that gradient line. It produces an image value, not an HTML element or JavaScript return value.
Use a gradient as decorative background. Keep text readable independently: this label has an opaque black backing. The color ramp is not the only way to communicate meaning.
Paint a navy-to-teal gradient toward the right, keeping the label backing.
after: A gradient is a gradual change between colors. `linear-gradient()` makes that change along a straight line. The browser creates the picture from CSS; you do not need an image file.

Inside `linear-gradient()`, commas separate the direction and color stops. A color stop gives a color and its place along the gradient. `navy 0%` puts navy at the start. `teal 100%` puts teal at the end.
Changing `to right` to `to bottom` makes the blend run downward. The endpoint colors stay the same. Use `to right` for this project.
Treat the gradient as decoration. Keep the label’s solid backing so the words stay easy to read across the whole banner. Do not use a color change as the only way to explain important information.
Check that the banner starts navy on the left and ends teal on the right. Keep the label’s white text and black backing, then run the checks.
